newsitem.title: DUBAI: Illegal aliens in UAE crowd on cargo ship home.
newsitem.headline: Illegal aliens in UAE crowd on cargo ship home.

text.p: More than 1,000 illegal aliens boarded a cargo ship in the United Arab Emirates on Monday for a five-day sea voyage to India, eager to leave for home ahead of a new law cracking down on unlawful foreign labour.

The passengers -- all men -- embarked after hours in line in the glaring sun, climbing up the narrow gangway onto the 3,500-tonnes Seawolf 103 with travel papers and tickets in hand. Their luggage was heaved onto the ship with a cargo crane.

Once on the boat, the men descended down narrow chutes into the dank, windowless hull of the ship, where they will sleep on two levels of wooden planks usually used to hold such cargoes as sugar and rice. On deck, workers have built 20 makeshift toilets -- wooden boxes with a hole set above a bucket.

The 1,300 people boarding the Seawolf are among an estimated 200,000 illegal workers scrambling to leave the oil-rich UAE, taking advantage of a government amnesty that gives them until October 31 to get their papers in order or get out.
Because of what the shipping agents called "hardship conditions", no women were allowed on board.
"It's all emergency arrangements," said the ship's agent Abdullah Kapadia. "You can't make heaven for the passengers. The only idea is to get them home cheap and safe."

Thousands of foreign workers -- primarily from the Indian subcontinent but also from southeast Asia -- have been rushing to leave the UAE by plane and small launches to avoid tough penalties when the new law takes effect on November 1.

Foreigners make up about 75 percent of the 2.4 million population in the small Gulf state. Many came to the Gulf legally, but broke the law by failing to leave when their visas expired or working for employers other than their sponsors. The government says they are a threat to the UAE's security.
If they are caught after the deadline, they face punishments including fines, prison terms and deportation.

The UAE estimates some 140,000 illegal aliens will depart during the three-month amnesty. Diplomats say as many as 200,000 could leave. But embassies said they had issued about 100,000 exit permits and the number of applicants was dwindling.
The Dubai airport authority said an average of 5,000 amnesty-seekers were departing through the airport every day.

As the sun began to set over Dubai's Hamriya Port, the men still waiting to board the Seawolf stood in orderly queues, wrapping masking tape around overstuffed cardboard boxes and wiping sweat from their necks and foreheads.

"It'll set sail in a few hours," said K.V. Shankar, head of the privately-funded Indian Association which organised the ship. "Tomorrow is the really big one with 2,300 passengers. That will leave from the port of Sharjah," Dubai's neighbouring emirate.

A man who gave his name only as Mutu carried nothing but a small plastic bag for his journey home. "This ship's no good because it's for cargo, not people," he said. "But I don't have any money so I don't have any choice."
